summary: Rainfall is not changing the same way everywhere on Earth: it can rise in one region while falling in another. Orvia is an interactive, bilingual (English/Arabic) web explorer that lets students and curious explorers investigate these opposite regional trends using 24 years (2001–2024) of NASA GPM IMERG satellite precipitation across eight study regions, starting from the Nile Delta. Users spin a 3D globe, pick a region, compare any year with its monthly baseline, and read the trend rate together with its uncertainty and statistical significance. "Find the Paradox" surfaces region pairs whose trends point in opposite directions (16 pairs in our baseline). Each region opens a detective case file: ten independent NASA clues (IMERG rain, a second MERRA-2 rain estimate, a water balance of rain minus evaporation, temperature, peak heat, soil moisture, humidity, evaporation, cloud cover and sunlight), each marked "confirmed" or "hint only", lead to a rule-based verdict (case closed, leaning, or open) that never claims more than the evidence supports. This answers the challenge by turning raw NASA Earth observations into an evidence-first detective workflow: spot a trend, test how certain it is, and decide what the data actually supports.
details:
What it does. Orvia shows how one Earth-system variable, precipitation, changes in different directions across the planet. A 3D globe built on NASA Blue Marble imagery marks eight regional study boxes (Nile Delta, Central Sahel, Southwest Australia, Eastern Amazon, Lake Victoria, Central Iberia, Western Borneo, Lower Paraná). For each region the explorer shows:

  • The annual precipitation series 2001–2024 with a selectable observation year and a monthly profile compared with the calendar-month baseline.
  • The trend rate in mm per decade (Theil–Sen), its 95% confidence interval, a Mann–Kendall test and a Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted q-value, so every number carries its uncertainty.
  • A side-by-side comparison of any two regions on shared axes.
  • "Find the Paradox": pairs of regions whose trends have opposite signs. The baseline finds 16 such pairs; all remain exploratory at the adjusted q ≤ 0.05 threshold, and the app says so explicitly instead of overstating the result.
  • A detective case file for every region: ten NASA clues, each with its rate of change, a "confirmed" (q ≤ 0.05) or "hint only" badge and its NASA source, plus a plain-language verdict. The case is closed only when the satellite rain trend is confirmed, leaning when all four water clues (IMERG rain, MERRA-2 rain, soil moisture, water balance) agree, and open otherwise. A built-in guide explains trend rate, q-value and correlation in simple words. In the current data, Lake Victoria, Western Borneo and Lower Paraná lean in a clear direction while the other five cases stay open, which shows students why one number is not proof.
  • A water balance (IMERG rain minus MERRA-2 land evaporation): the water actually left for soil and rivers. In the Nile Delta, rain rose slightly while the water balance fell, because evaporation grew faster.
  • Climate signals from NASA POWER: 2 m air temperature, peak temperature, root-zone soil wetness, relative humidity, land evaporation, cloud cover, surface solar radiation, and MERRA-2 bias-corrected precipitation as an independent cross-check. Six of eight regions warmed with strong evidence; the second rain estimate agrees with IMERG on the direction of change in seven regions; soil moisture tracks rainfall in every region.
  • A methodology page, downloadable regional CSVs, and a read-only JSON API (/api/v1/regions, trends, paradoxes, timeseries, signals, variables, metadata, health).
  • A full English and Arabic interface.

How it works. An offline, reproducible Python pipeline downloads the original NASA IMERG V07B monthly grids (via the NSF NCAR GDEX byte-range index), verifies units and granule IDs, selects the grid cells inside each box, computes cosine-latitude-weighted regional means, converts mm/hr to monthly depth, keeps only complete years, and computes the statistics. Every output records source URLs, dataset version and SHA-256 hashes. We independently recomputed all eight December 2024 regional totals from the full HDF5 granule and matched them to 10⁻¹² relative tolerance. A second script fetches the NASA POWER monthly API for the same boxes. The results ship as static data to a Next.js / React / TypeScript frontend with a WebGL globe and Plotly charts.

Tools. Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, pytest) with custom HDF5 chunk decoding, Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, three.js / React Three Fiber for the WebGL globe, Plotly.js charts, GSAP animation, Zod schemas, Playwright end-to-end tests, GitHub Actions CI, Azure App Service hosting.

Limits we state in the app. Spatial averaging over boxes, natural climate variability, possible serial dependence and satellite retrieval uncertainty all limit interpretation. The tool shows correlation and trend evidence, not causes.

Why it matters. Climate headlines often generalize ("it is getting drier"). Orvia teaches users to look regionally, check uncertainty, and only claim what the evidence supports, using open NASA data anyone can reproduce.

Use of AI tools. OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude helped write and review the source code, interface copy, Arabic translation, tests and documentation. The team reviewed and directed all output. No AI-generated images, video, audio or data are included; every number is computed by our Python pipeline from NASA observations.
